cues.t: Phages are viruses that hunt bacteria.
They have been doing it for billions of years.
That matters right now.
Antibiotic resistance is rising,
and infections we could once cure are becoming untreatable.
Phages are one way to fight back,
but only if a phage can infect the exact bacterium
making someone sick.
Most of the time, it cannot.
That decision is made in the first seconds of contact,
by the tail spike proteins that grip the bacterial surface.
We do not know which parts of them set the host range,
and we cannot yet aim a phage at a new host.
We are Phagenomics, a team from Claremont, California.
We isolated our phages from water and soil we sampled,
along with the bacteria they infect,
and sequenced them ourselves.
We treat host range as an evolutionary question.
We take the receptor binding protein,
the part that makes first contact,
and reconstruct its ancestors,
versions that existed long before the strains on our bench.
We build those ancestral proteins in the lab
and measure how tightly each one binds its target.
Evolution already ran this experiment.
The ancestral sequences are its notes,
recording which changes opened a host range
and which closed it.
Those measurements train our model,
and the model tells us what to change next.
So this is a time machine.
We go backward to find out what evolution learned,
and we run it forward to design
the next generation of phages.
